questions.q: If A = {a, b}, write down P(A) explicitly using correct set notation.
questions.a: P(A) = {φ, {a}, {b}, {a, b}}. A wrong answer like {{a}, {b}, {a, b}} (missing φ) reveals the student doesn't grasp that the empty set is a subset of *every* set. Writing {a, b, φ} (missing braces) reveals confusion between elements and subsets — they treat φ as an element of A rather than a subset.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why n(P(A)) = 2^n for a finite set A with n elements. Use the concept of "choices" for each element.
questions.a: Each element of A has exactly two independent choices: either it is included in a subset or it is not. By the Fundamental Principle of Counting, total subsets = 2 × 2 × ... × 2 (n times) = 2^n. A wrong answer like "because there are n elements and we double them" shows they memorized the formula without understanding the combinatorial reasoning. Saying "2^n includes the set itself" confuses the count with the content.

questions.q: Let A = {1, {2, 3}}. Find P(A) and state n(P(A)).
questions.a:
A has 2 elements: 1 and {2, 3}. So n(P(A)) = 2^2 = 4.
P(A) = {φ, {1}, {{2, 3}}, {1, {2, 3}}}.
A wrong answer like {φ, {1}, {2, 3}, {1, 2, 3}} reveals the critical misconception: treating {2, 3} as if its elements (2, 3) belong to A. They fail to see {2, 3} is a *single element* (a set) of A, not two separate elements.

questions.q: Compare P(A) and P(B) where A = {1, 2} and B = {1, 2, 3}. Is P(A) a subset of P(B)? Is P(A) an element of P(B)? Justify both answers.
questions.a: P(A) = {φ, {1}, {2}, {1, 2}}. P(B) has 8 elements including all of P(A)'s elements. So P(A) ⊆ P(B) — YES, every subset of A is also a subset of B. But P(A) ∉ P(B) — NO, because elements of P(B) are subsets of B (like {1, 2}), not sets of subsets. A wrong "YES" to the second reveals confusion between ⊆ (subset) and ∈ (element of). They think "P(A) is a set, so it can be an element" without checking if it's a subset of B.

questions.q: A student claims: "If n(A) = 3, then n(P(P(A))) = 2^3 = 8." Evaluate this claim. Is it correct? If not, find the correct value and explain the error.
questions.a:
The claim is INCORRECT.
n(A) = 3 → n(P(A)) = 2^3 = 8.
Then n(P(P(A))) = 2^{n(P(A))} = 2^8 = 256.
The student applied the formula only once, treating P(P(A)) as if it were P(A). They failed to recognize the nesting: the outer power set acts on a set of size 8, not 3. This reveals a lack of hierarchical thinking about sets of sets.

questions.q: Create your own example of a set C (with n(C) = 3) such that one element of C is itself a set with 2 elements. Write P(C) and circle the elements of P(C) that are "nested sets" (i.e., sets containing a set as an element).
questions.a:
Example: C = {x, y, {p, q}}.
P(C) = {φ, {x}, {y}, {{p, q}}, {x, y}, {x, {p, q}}, {y, {p, q}}, {x, y, {p, q}}}.
The nested sets (elements containing {p, q}) are: {{p, q}}, {x, {p, q}}, {y, {p, q}}, {x, y, {p, q}} — 4 of them.
A poor answer uses C = {1, 2, 3} (no nested set) or writes P(C) incorrectly by "expanding" {p, q}. This reveals they cannot construct sets with sets as elements, a prerequisite for understanding P(P(A)).
